report.answer_text:
Presbyopia is the age-related loss of near focusing. It usually starts in the early to mid 40s. The lens stiffens and the eye can no longer change focus easily. It can't be prevented or reversed, but it can be corrected in several ways.
Non-surgical options
Reading glasses. These are the simplest choice. They are good if you only need help up close.
Bifocals, trifocals, or progressive lenses. These put distance and near correction in a single pair of glasses. Progressives have no visible lines.
Multifocal or monovision contact lenses. Multifocal lenses have several focus zones. With monovision, one eye is corrected for distance and the other for near.
Occupational or computer glasses. These are tuned for intermediate and near work.
Prescription eye drops. Some newer drops, such as pilocarpine-based ones, shrink the pupil to increase depth of focus. They help some people temporarily and can have side effects like dim vision or headaches. Ask an eye doctor whether they suit you.
Surgical and procedural options
Refractive lens exchange. The natural lens is replaced with a multifocal or extended-depth-of-focus intraocular lens. This is also what's done in cataract surgery, and it can reduce or remove the need for glasses.
Accommodating IOLs. These lenses are designed to shift a little and give some range of focus.
Laser monovision LASIK or PRK. One eye is set for near vision and the other for distance.
Corneal inlays. A small implant in one eye increases depth of focus. These are less common now, and some have been withdrawn from the market.
Conductive keratoplasty. Radiofrequency energy reshapes the cornea. It's used less often today.
Things to keep in mind
Presbyopia keeps progressing until about age 60–65. Glasses prescriptions often need updating every few years.
Surgical options can cause glare, halos, or less sharp contrast. They aren't right for everyone.
Get an eye exam to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other problems. An eye care professional can help you pick the option that fits your lifestyle, job, and eye health.
I can go into more detail on any of these if you'd like.
